prompt:
What is logged? 
console.log(x);
var x = 5;
explanation: var declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope and initialized to undefined; only the assignment (x = 5) stays in place. So console.log(x) runs after the hoisted declaration but before the assignment, logging undefined rather than throwing.

prompt: Which keyword allows reassignment but not redeclaration in the same scope, and is block-scoped?
explanation: let creates a block-scoped binding that can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope, unlike var (function-scoped, redeclarable) and const (block-scoped but not reassignable).

prompt:
What happens here? 
console.log(y);
let y = 10;
choices: ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone
explanation: let and const bindings exist in the 'temporal dead zone' from the start of their block until their declaration is evaluated; accessing them before that point throws a ReferenceError instead of returning undefined.

prompt: What is the scope of a variable declared with var inside a for-loop block { } inside a function?
explanation: var is function-scoped (or global-scoped), not block-scoped, so a var declared inside a for-loop's { } is hoisted to the enclosing function and remains accessible after the loop block ends.

var creates a single binding shared across all loop iterations, so by the time the setTimeout callbacks run (after the loop has finished), i has already reached its final value of 3 in every callback.

prompt: A closure is:
choices: A function bundled together with references to its surrounding state
A synchronous version of a promise
A way to close a file handle
explanation: A closure is a function combined with references to its surrounding lexical scope, letting it read and update variables from an outer function even after that function has returned.

Each call to counter() creates a new count variable captured by the returned arrow function's closure. ++count increments and returns the value, so three sequential calls log 1, 2, 3 in the order the console.log arguments are evaluated.

prompt: The classic "var in a loop with setTimeout" closure bug can be fixed by:
explanation: Replacing var with let gives the loop a fresh, block-scoped binding of i for every iteration, so each setTimeout callback closes over its own copy instead of sharing one variable.
Because the loop uses let, each iteration gets its own binding of i, so each arrow function pushed into adders closes over a different value (0, 1, 2), producing 10, 11, 12 when called with 10.

prompt: Which statement about closures and memory is true?
choices: Closures can prevent garbage collection of variables they still reference
Closures are always garbage collected immediately after the outer function returns
Closures cannot access variables from an outer function once it has returned
Closures only work with arrow functions
explanation: As long as a closure still references a variable from its outer scope, that variable can't be garbage collected even after the outer function has returned — closures keep their captured environment alive.

prompt: In a regular (non-arrow) function called as a plain function in non-strict mode, this refers to:
explanation: In non-strict mode, calling a regular function without an explicit receiver sets this to the global object (globalThis / window in browsers); strict mode would instead leave it undefined.

prompt: Arrow functions differ from regular functions in that they:
choices: Do not have their own this; they inherit it from the enclosing scope
Always bind this to the global object
explanation: Arrow functions don't have their own this binding; they lexically capture this from the enclosing scope at the time they're defined, which is why they're commonly used to preserve this inside callbacks.

The arrow function () => this.value has no this of its own, so it inherits this from getValue's enclosing execution — which is obj, since getValue is called as obj.getValue(). That makes this.value resolve to 42.

prompt: Which method explicitly sets this for a function call and invokes it immediately?
explanation: Function.prototype.call invokes the function immediately with a given this value and individually listed arguments, unlike bind (which returns a new function) or apply (which takes arguments as an array).

choices: The regular function callback loses the class instance's this binding
explanation: The callback passed to setInterval is a regular function invoked without a receiver, so its own this is not the Timer instance — it defaults to the global object (or undefined in strict mode), which has no seconds property.

prompt: Every JS object has an internal link to another object called its:
explanation: Every JS object carries an internal link, [[Prototype]] (exposed via Object.getPrototypeOf or the deprecated __proto__), to another object it inherits properties from — its prototype.

prompt: What does Object.create(proto) do?
choices: Creates a new object with proto as its prototype
Clones proto's own properties into a new object
explanation: Object.create(proto) builds a brand-new object whose [[Prototype]] is set to proto, without copying proto's own properties onto it.

prompt: In class Dog extends Animal {}, which built-in mechanism does extends use under the hood?
explanation: class ... extends sets up prototype chaining under the hood: Dog.prototype's [[Prototype]] becomes Animal.prototype, so Dog instances inherit Animal's methods through the prototype chain.

prompt: What does the instanceof operator check?
choices: Whether an object's prototype chain includes the constructor's prototype
Whether two objects have identical own properties
Whether a variable's typeof matches a string
explanation: a instanceof B checks whether B.prototype appears anywhere in a's prototype chain, not whether a and B share identical own properties.

choices: TypeError: a.speak is not a function
explanation: delete a.speak only removes the own property speak from a — speak still exists on Animal.prototype, so property lookup falls through the prototype chain and finds it there, logging 'Rex makes a noise.'

prompt: A Promise can be in one of three states:
explanation: A Promise is always in exactly one of three states — pending (not yet settled), fulfilled (resolved with a value), or rejected (failed with a reason) — and can only transition from pending to one of the other two, once.

prompt: What does await do inside an async function?
choices: Pauses execution of that function until the awaited promise settles
Blocks the entire JS engine synchronously
Converts a promise into a callback
explanation: await suspends execution of the enclosing async function until the awaited promise settles, without blocking the rest of the JS runtime — other code can still run via the event loop in the meantime.
All synchronous code runs first, so 'A' and 'C' log before the microtask queued by .then() is processed after the current call stack empties — giving the order A, C, B.

Synchronous code ('start', 'end') runs first; then, once the call stack is empty, the microtask queue (the Promise .then callback) is fully drained before the macrotask queue (the setTimeout callback) runs — giving start, end, promise, timeout.

prompt: What does Promise.allSettled return, compared to Promise.all?
choices: An array of result objects for every promise, regardless of rejection, instead of rejecting on the first failure
Nothing, it behaves identically to Promise.all
explanation: Promise.allSettled waits for every promise to settle and resolves with an array of {status, value|reason} results for each one, whereas Promise.all rejects immediately as soon as any single promise rejects.

prompt: Which queue is processed first after the current synchronous code finishes: the microtask queue or the macrotask (timer) queue?
choices: Whichever was registered first, regardless of type
explanation: Once the current synchronous code finishes, the JS runtime fully drains the microtask queue (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before moving on to the next macrotask (timers, I/O).

prompt: setTimeout(fn, 0) guarantees:
choices: fn runs on the next available macrotask tick, not immediately
fn runs before any Promise callbacks
explanation: setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run fn immediately — it schedules fn as a macrotask for the next tick of the event loop, which only happens after the current call stack (and any pending microtasks) finish.

prompt: Which of these schedules a microtask?
explanation: Promise.prototype.then schedules its callback as a microtask, run after the current synchronous code and before the next macrotask; setTimeout, setInterval, and requestAnimationFrame all schedule macrotask-style callbacks instead.

prompt: Why can a long, purely synchronous loop block UI updates and timer callbacks in a single-threaded JS runtime?
choices: The event loop cannot process the callback/microtask queues until the current call stack is empty
Timers run on the same thread and always execute exactly on schedule regardless of blocking code
Synchronous code always runs after all callbacks
JS automatically pauses loops longer than 1 second
explanation: The event loop can only pull the next callback off the microtask/macrotask queues once the call stack is completely empty, so a long synchronous loop keeps the stack busy and blocks all pending timers, promise callbacks, and UI updates until it finishes.

prompt: What best describes the "call stack" in the JS runtime model?
choices: A LIFO structure tracking function calls currently executing
A queue of pending network requests
The list of all variables in global scope
A cache of previously resolved promises
explanation: The call stack is a LIFO (last-in, first-out) structure that tracks the currently executing function calls, pushing a new frame on each call and popping it off when that function returns.

prompt: Which array method creates a new array with the results of calling a function on every element?
explanation: Array.prototype.map calls a function on every element and returns a new array of the results, leaving the original array unchanged.

prompt: Which method returns a new array containing only the elements that satisfy a condition?
explanation: Array.prototype.filter returns a new array containing only the elements for which the callback returns a truthy value.

prompt: What does [1, 2, 3].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0) evaluate to?
explanation: reduce runs the callback for each element, carrying an accumulator forward: starting at 0, it computes 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6, so the final result is 6.

prompt: What's the key difference between forEach and map?
choices: map returns a new array; forEach returns undefined
map mutates the original array; forEach does not
explanation: map returns a brand-new array built from the callback's return values, while forEach always returns undefined and is used purely for side effects; neither method mutates the original array.

prompt:
What does this log? 
console.log([1, [2, 3], [4, [5, 6]]].flat(Infinity));
choices: Error: flat requires a numeric argument
explanation: flat(depth) flattens nested arrays up to the given depth; passing Infinity flattens arbitrarily deep nesting, so every nested array collapses into a single flat array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

prompt:
What does the following produce? 
const { a, b } = { a: 1, b: 2 };
choices: a and b are both undefined
explanation: Object destructuring const { a, b } = obj pulls the a and b properties off the right-hand object and binds them to local variables of the same name, so a is 1 and b is 2.

prompt: What does const { a, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }; assign to rest?
explanation: The rest pattern (...rest) in a destructuring assignment collects whatever own enumerable properties weren't already destructured into a new object, so rest becomes { b: 2, c: 3 }.

prompt: How do you destructure obj.name, binding it to a local variable n?
explanation: const { name: n } = obj destructures the name property but binds it to a local variable called n instead of name — the syntax reads as 'property: localName'.

prompt: What does Object.freeze(obj) do?
choices: Prevents adding, removing, or reassigning obj's own properties (shallowly)
explanation: Object.freeze(obj) prevents adding new properties, removing existing ones, and reassigning existing property values on obj — but only shallowly, at the top level.
Object.freeze only freezes an object's own top-level properties, not nested objects it references. Since nested is a separate object, frozen.nested.b = 99 succeeds and logs 99.

prompt: What does the spread operator do in const arr2 = [...arr1, 4, 5];?
choices: Copies arr1's elements into a new array, followed by 4 and 5
Merges arr1 and arr2 by reference
explanation: The spread operator (...arr1) expands arr1's elements in place, so [...arr1, 4, 5] builds a brand-new array containing arr1's elements followed by 4 and 5.

prompt: Template literals are delimited by:
explanation: Template literals are delimited by backticks (`), which also enable ${...} interpolation and multi-line strings — unlike single or double quotes.

prompt:
What value does name take here? 
function greet(name = 'World') { return `Hello ${name}`; }
greet(undefined);
explanation: Default parameter values are used whenever the argument is undefined — either omitted entirely or explicitly passed as undefined — so greet(undefined) uses the default 'World'.

choices: Collects all remaining arguments into an array called nums
Is only valid for object destructuring
explanation: The rest parameter syntax (...nums) gathers all remaining arguments passed to the function into a single real array called nums.

prompt: What is a key difference between Object.entries(obj) and using a for...in loop directly on obj?
choices: for...in also iterates inherited enumerable properties from the prototype chain, while Object.entries only includes own enumerable properties
for...in is faster in all engines
Object.entries cannot be used with arrays
explanation: for...in walks every enumerable property key, including ones inherited from the prototype chain, while Object.entries(obj) only returns the object's own enumerable [key, value] pairs.

prompt: What does '5' == 5 evaluate to?
explanation: == performs type coercion before comparing, so '5' is converted to the number 5, making '5' == 5 evaluate to true.

prompt: What does '5' === 5 evaluate to?
explanation: === (strict equality) never coerces types, so a string and a number are always unequal regardless of their apparent value — '5' === 5 is false.

prompt: What does NaN === NaN evaluate to, and what should you use instead to check for NaN?
choices: false; there is no way to check for NaN
explanation: NaN is the only JS value that is never equal to itself, so NaN === NaN is false; Number.isNaN(x) (unlike the coercing global isNaN) reliably checks for NaN without false positives on non-numeric values.

prompt: What does [] == false evaluate to?
explanation: With ==, [] is coerced to a primitive first (via toString → ''), then '' and false are both coerced to the number 0 for comparison, so [] == false evaluates to true.

prompt: What does Object.is(NaN, NaN) return, and how does it differ from === regarding -0 and +0?
choices: true for NaN, and Object.is distinguishes -0 from +0 (unlike ===)
false for NaN, identical to === in every case
true for NaN, but treats -0 and +0 as unequal only when using ===
Object.is does not exist in JavaScript
explanation: Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true (unlike ===, which treats NaN as unequal to itself), and it also distinguishes -0 from +0, whereas === considers -0 === +0 to be true.

prompt: Which TypeScript type represents any JavaScript value with no type checking at all (opts out of type safety)?
explanation: any disables type checking entirely for a value — you can assign it anything and access any property or method on it without the compiler complaining, unlike unknown, which still requires narrowing.

prompt: What must you do before using a value's properties when its type is unknown, unlike any?
choices: Perform a type check or type assertion to narrow it first
Nothing, it behaves exactly like any
It can only hold string values
explanation: unknown is the type-safe counterpart to any: TypeScript won't let you access properties, call methods, or otherwise operate on an unknown value until you've narrowed it with a type guard or assertion.

prompt: What type would you give a function that never returns normally (e.g. it always throws)?
explanation: never represents a value that can't occur — it's the correct return type for a function that always throws or otherwise never completes normally, since it never actually produces a return value.

prompt: What is the difference between void and undefined as a function return type?
choices: void means the return value should be ignored; undefined means the function explicitly returns the value undefined
They are functionally different keywords for numbers
void can only be used on classes
There is no difference at all
explanation: void means a function's return value is meaningless and callers shouldn't rely on it (even if it technically returns undefined), whereas a return type of undefined asserts the function explicitly returns that literal value.

prompt: Given let x: unknown = 'hello';, which of the following compiles without a type assertion or narrowing first?
explanation: typeof works on any value regardless of its static type, so typeof x compiles fine on an unknown. Accessing x.toUpperCase(), x.length, or doing arithmetic on x all require narrowing unknown to a more specific type first.

prompt: Which keyword defines a named object shape that supports declaration merging (multiple declarations combining)?
explanation: interface defines a named object shape and, unlike type, supports declaration merging — multiple interface declarations with the same name are automatically combined into one.

prompt: Can a type alias represent a union of primitive types (e.g. string | number)?
choices: Yes, type aliases support unions directly; interfaces cannot
Yes, but interfaces support it identically
explanation: type aliases can represent any type, including unions like string | number, directly; interfaces can only describe object (and function/constructor) shapes, not unions of primitives.

prompt: How do you extend an interface to add more properties?
explanation: interface B extends A { } makes B inherit all of A's members, adding whatever additional members are declared in B's own body.

prompt: What does declaration merging allow you to do with two interface Foo declarations in the same scope?
choices: Their members are automatically combined into one interface
The second declaration throws a duplicate identifier error
Only the second declaration is used, the first is ignored
TypeScript requires renaming one of them
explanation: Declaration merging means multiple interface Foo declarations in the same scope aren't errors or overwrites — TypeScript automatically merges their members into a single combined interface.

prompt: What's the idiomatic way to combine two object types with type (since extends isn't available on type aliases)?
explanation: Since type aliases can't use extends, the idiomatic way to combine two object types is an intersection (type C = A & B), which produces a type that has all the members of both A and B.

prompt: What is the purpose of a generic type parameter like in function identity(arg: T): T?
choices: It lets the function work with any type while preserving type information through input and output
It forces the function to only accept numbers
It disables type checking for the function
It marks the function as asynchronous
explanation: A generic type parameter like <T> lets a function work with whatever type is passed in while preserving that exact type through to the return value, instead of widening it to any or a fixed type.

prompt: What does T extends U mean in a generic constraint like function f(arg: T)?
choices: T must be a type that is assignable to (has at least the shape of) U
T can never be U's subtype
explanation: T extends U in a generic constraint restricts T to types that are structurally assignable to U — i.e. T must have at least the shape U requires — not that T must be exactly U.

prompt: Given function firstElement(arr: T[]): T | undefined { return arr[0]; }, what does calling firstElement([1, 2, 3]) infer T as?
choices: T is left unresolved and must be specified manually
explanation: TypeScript infers generic type arguments from how a function is called. Passing [1, 2, 3] (a number[]) lets it infer T as number, so the return type becomes number | undefined.

choices: It returns the type of the property at key K on object type T, ensuring key is a valid key of T
It always returns type T regardless of key
It throws a compile error because keyof cannot be used in generics
It converts obj into an array of its keys
explanation: K extends keyof T constrains key to only the valid property names of T, and the indexed access type T[K] then gives the precise type of that property — so wrap returns exactly the type of obj[key].
Explicit type arguments pair<string, number>('a', 1) substitute A = string and B = number directly into the return type [A, B], giving a concrete tuple return type of [string, number].

prompt: What does the union type string | number mean for a variable's allowed values?
choices: The variable can hold either a string or a number
The variable must hold both a string and a number simultaneously
The variable can only hold string values
explanation: A union type string | number means a value must be one type or the other (though not necessarily known which until it's narrowed) — it does not mean both simultaneously.

prompt: What does the intersection type A & B require of a value?
choices: It must satisfy the members of both A and B simultaneously
It must satisfy either A or B
It converts A into B at runtime
It is only valid for primitive types
explanation: An intersection type A & B requires a value to satisfy the members of both A and B at the same time, effectively combining their properties into one type.

prompt: Given type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error';, what is this pattern called?
explanation: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error' is a union of string literal types — each member is a specific, exact string value rather than the general string type.

choices: No error — value must have both x (number) and y (string)
Error — A and B cannot be intersected
No error, but value is typed as never
explanation: A & B is an intersection, so a value assigned to it must satisfy both A and B at once — it needs both an x: number and a y: string — which { x: 1, y: 'hi' } does, so this compiles without error.

prompt: Why does type Impossible = { a: string } & { a: number }; result in the property a having type never?
choices: Because the intersection requires a to satisfy both string and number simultaneously, which no value can, so TypeScript resolves it to never
Because TypeScript disallows intersecting object types entirely
Because string and number are considered identical types
explanation: Intersecting { a: string } & { a: number } requires a to be assignable to both string and number simultaneously. No value satisfies both, so TypeScript resolves that property's type to never — the type with no possible values.

choices: Narrow value's type to string inside the if-block, enabling string methods
Nothing, typeof has no effect on TypeScript's type checking
Convert value into a string at runtime
Throw a compile error because value is a union type
explanation: TypeScript recognizes typeof value === 'string' as a type guard and narrows value's static type to string for the rest of that block, so calling value.toUpperCase() type-checks.
The in operator, used as a type guard ('swim' in pet), lets TypeScript narrow pet to whichever union member actually has that property — here, Fish — inside the if-block.

choices: Discriminated union narrowing via a common literal tag property
Structural duck typing with no compile-time checks
explanation: Shape is a discriminated union: each member shares a common literal 'tag' property (kind) with a distinct value, letting TypeScript narrow to the exact member based on a check like s.kind === 'circle'.

choices: Calling isString(x) narrows x's type to string in the branch where it returns true
It converts any value into a string
It disables type checking for value
explanation: A function with a `value is Type` return type is a user-defined type guard. When isString(x) returns true, TypeScript narrows x's type to string within that branch, just like a built-in typeof check.

prompt: Given function assertIsNumber(val: unknown): asserts val is number { if (typeof val !== 'number') throw new Error(); }, what happens to val's type after a call to this function that doesn't throw?
choices: TypeScript narrows val's type to number for the rest of that scope
Nothing, assertion functions don't affect types, only runtime behavior
It converts val into a string
It only works inside generic functions
explanation: An assertion function declared with `asserts val is number` tells TypeScript that, if the call returns without throwing, val can be narrowed to number for the rest of the enclosing scope.

prompt: Which built-in utility type makes all properties of a type optional?
explanation: Partial<T> produces a new type with every property of T made optional, useful for representing partial updates to an object.

prompt: Which utility type makes all properties of a type required, even if originally optional?
explanation: Required<T> is the opposite of Partial<T> — it produces a type where every property of T is mandatory, even ones originally declared optional.

prompt: What does Pick produce?
choices: A type with only the properties a and b from T
A type with all properties of T except a and b
explanation: Pick<T, K> constructs a new type containing only the properties named in the union K, so Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> keeps just a and b from T.

prompt: What does Omit produce?
choices: A type with all of T's properties except a
A type with only property a
A type where a is optional
A type where a becomes readonly
explanation: Omit<T, K> is the inverse of Pick — it constructs a type with all of T's properties except the ones named in K, so Omit<T, 'a'> keeps everything but a.

prompt: What does Record<'a' | 'b', number> produce?
choices: A number that is either a or b
A type error, Record cannot take a union
explanation: Record<K, T> builds an object type whose keys are the members of union K, each mapped to type T, so Record<'a' | 'b', number> is equivalent to { a: number; b: number }.

prompt: What does a numeric TypeScript enum default its member values to, if not explicitly assigned?
explanation: In a numeric enum, members without an explicit value default to auto-incrementing integers starting at 0 for the first member.

prompt: What is a key difference between a const enum and a regular enum?
choices: const enum members are fully inlined at compile time and produce no runtime object
const enum values can be reassigned at runtime
const enum only supports string values
explanation: const enum members are inlined directly at their usage sites during compilation and don't generate a runtime lookup object at all, unlike a regular enum, which compiles to an actual JS object.

prompt: What do string enums provide that numeric enums don't?
choices: More meaningful, self-documenting runtime values instead of arbitrary numbers, with no reverse mapping generated
Faster runtime performance in all cases
The ability to mix types within the same member
explanation: String enum members must be initialized with string literals, giving each member a meaningful, self-documenting runtime value — and unlike numeric enums, string enums don't generate a reverse mapping.

prompt: Given enum Direction { Up, Down }, what does the compiled JavaScript's reverse mapping allow?
choices: Looking up the member name from its numeric value at runtime (e.g. Direction[0] === 'Up')
Converting the enum into a string enum automatically
Preventing any runtime access to enum values
Making the enum immutable by default
explanation: Numeric enums compile with a reverse mapping, so you can look up a member's name from its numeric value at runtime — e.g. Direction[0] evaluates to the string 'Up'.

prompt: Why do many TypeScript style guides recommend a union of string literals (e.g. type Direction = 'up' | 'down') over enums in some cases?
choices: Literal unions have no runtime footprint and avoid enum-specific quirks like reverse mappings, while still providing type safety
Because enums are deprecated and no longer supported
Because literal unions support more values than enums
Because enums cannot be used in switch statements
explanation: A union of string literals compiles away entirely — it has zero runtime footprint — and sidesteps enum-specific quirks like numeric reverse mappings, while TypeScript still enforces that only the listed values are valid.

prompt: Which access modifier restricts a class member to being visible only within the declaring class itself?
explanation: private restricts a class member so it's only accessible from within the declaring class itself — not from subclasses and not from outside code.

prompt: Which access modifier allows a member to be accessed by the declaring class and its subclasses, but not from outside?
explanation: protected allows a member to be accessed from the declaring class and any of its subclasses, but not from outside the class hierarchy — a middle ground between private and public.

prompt: What does the readonly modifier on a class property enforce?
choices: The property can only be assigned once (typically in the constructor) and not reassigned afterward
The property cannot be read outside the class
The property must always be a primitive
explanation: readonly enforces that a property can only be assigned once — typically in the constructor — after which any further assignment is a compile-time error.

Adding an access modifier (like private) directly to a constructor parameter is TypeScript's parameter property shorthand — it both declares the class property and assigns it from the argument in one step.

prompt: What is the difference between an abstract class and a regular class, regarding instantiation?
choices: An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly and may declare methods without implementations that subclasses must implement
Abstract classes can only contain static methods
Abstract classes are identical to interfaces in every way, including at runtime
explanation: An abstract class can't be instantiated directly with new — it exists to be subclassed — and it may declare abstract methods with no implementation that concrete subclasses are required to implement.

prompt: How do you type a function parameter as optional in TypeScript?
explanation: Appending ? after a parameter name, as in function f(name?: string) {}, marks that parameter as optional, meaning callers may omit it entirely.

prompt: What does a function overload signature let you express that a single generic signature can't easily?
choices: Different parameter/return type combinations for the same function name, each checked independently
explanation: Overload signatures let you declare several distinct parameter/return type combinations for the same function name, each checked independently by callers, which a single generic signature often can't express precisely.

prompt: What does typing a callback parameter as (value: number) => void communicate?
choices: The callback takes a number argument and its return value is ignored
The callback must return a number
explanation: A function type (value: number) => void describes a callback that must accept a number argument and whose return value is expected to be ignored by the caller.

choices: To give callers precise, type-specific return types (string in, string out; T[] in, T[] out) while sharing one implementation
To allow the function to accept unlimited argument counts
To make the function generic only for arrays
To disable type checking on the implementation signature
explanation: These overload signatures give callers precise, input-specific return types — a string argument yields a string return, and a T[] argument yields a T[] return — while a single, loosely-typed implementation signature handles both cases at runtime.

choices: It documents and type-checks what this should be when the method is called, without being a real runtime parameter
It declares a real parameter that callers must pass explicitly
It is ignored entirely by the compiler
explanation: A this parameter in a function/method signature is a compile-time-only construct that documents and type-checks what this must be when the method is invoked; it is erased during compilation and isn't a real parameter callers pass.

prompt: What does the keyof operator produce when applied to a type?
choices: A union of the type's property names as string (or symbol) literal types
An array of the type's values
The number of properties on the type
explanation: keyof T produces a union of all of T's property names as string (or symbol/number) literal types, which is commonly used to constrain generic key parameters.

prompt: What does typeof do when used in a type position (not a value position), e.g. type T = typeof someVariable?
choices: Extracts the static type of someVariable for reuse as a type
Returns the runtime string 'object' or similar
explanation: Used in a type position, typeof someVariable extracts the static TypeScript type that was inferred for someVariable, letting you reuse it as a type elsewhere — this is distinct from the runtime typeof operator.

choices: A version of T with every property marked readonly, otherwise identical
A version of T with every property removed
A version of T where all values become strings
An error, mapped types cannot use readonly
explanation: This mapped type iterates every key K in keyof T and re-declares each property with the readonly modifier while keeping its original type T[K], producing a fully read-only version of T.

choices: A is true, B is false
A is false, B is true
Both A and B are true
Both A and B are never
explanation: Conditional types evaluate T extends string ? true : false per type argument: 'hello' is assignable to string, so A is true; 42 is not, so B is false.

prompt:
What does infer do inside a conditional type, as shown here?
